```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(epifitter)
library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)
theme_set(cowplot::theme_half_open(font_size = 12))
```

## Overview

The `sim_` family creates synthetic disease progress curves that match the same model families used by the fitting functions.

Simulations are useful for teaching, testing analysis workflows, checking
whether a model can recover known parameters, and generating reproducible
examples. They are not a substitute for biological validation. Choose parameter
values that make sense for the host-pathogen system, disease metric, and time
scale.

## Read the simulation output

Each simulator evaluates an analytical curve at `seq(0, N, by = dt)` and returns:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `replicates` | Replicate identifier, from 1 to `n` |
| `time` | Assessment time; the last time can be less than `N` if `dt` does not divide it evenly |
| `y` | Underlying deterministic disease progress curve |
| `random_y` | Replicated observations after adding noise and applying the bounds below |

Replicates share the same curve parameters; `n` does not introduce variation
in infection rates, initial intensities, or asymptotes. Use `set.seed()` for
reproducible observations and `alpha = 0` to turn off the added noise.

## Understand observation noise

Before clipping, observations are independent normal draws centered on `y`.
The noise parameter `alpha` controls their standard deviation:

- Exponential: `alpha * y`.
- Monomolecular, logistic, and Gompertz: `alpha * y * (1 - y)`.

All four simulators replace draws below `y0` with `y0`. The three bounded
models also replace draws above 1 with 0.999, then apply the lower bound at
`y0`. Clipping changes the observation distribution near these limits, so
the final observations need not have mean exactly `y`.

`K` bounds the underlying curve of the three bounded models. Noisy observations
can exceed `K`; the upper observation bound is 1, rather than `K`.
Exponential curves and observations can exceed 1. If exponential growth or
noise exceeds the finite numeric range, the simulator stops; reduce `N`, `r`,
or `alpha`.

## Simulate four canonical curve shapes

The four model families represent different epidemic shapes. Exponential
growth is most appropriate for early unconstrained increase, while
monomolecular, logistic, and Gompertz curves include different forms of
deceleration as disease approaches an upper limit.

```{r}
set.seed(1)

exp_model <- sim_exponential(N = 100, y0 = 0.01, dt = 10, r = 0.045, alpha = 0.2, n = 5)
mono_model <- sim_monomolecular(N = 100, y0 = 0.01, dt = 5, r = 0.05, alpha = 0.2, n = 5)
log_model <- sim_logistic(N = 100, y0 = 0.01, dt = 5, r = 0.10, alpha = 0.2, n = 5)
gomp_model <- sim_gompertz(N = 100, y0 = 0.01, dt = 5, r = 0.07, alpha = 0.2, n = 5)
```

```{r}
exp_plot <- ggplot(exp_model, aes(time, y)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = random_y), width = 0.1, color = "#6c757d") +
  geom_line(color = "#b56576", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Exponential")

mono_plot <- ggplot(mono_model, aes(time, y)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = random_y), width = 0.1, color = "#6c757d") +
  geom_line(color = "#588157", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Monomolecular")

log_plot <- ggplot(log_model, aes(time, y)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = random_y), width = 0.1, color = "#6c757d") +
  geom_line(color = "#355070", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Logistic")

gomp_plot <- ggplot(gomp_model, aes(time, y)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = random_y), width = 0.1, color = "#6c757d") +
  geom_line(color = "#8d5a97", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Gompertz")
```

```{r fig.height=6, fig.width=8, fig.alt="Grid of four simulated disease progress curves showing exponential, monomolecular, logistic, and Gompertz shapes."}
plot_grid(exp_plot, mono_plot, log_plot, gomp_plot, ncol = 2)
```

## Send simulated data into the fitting pipeline

```{r}
fit_from_sim <- fit_lin(time = log_model$time, y = log_model$random_y)
fit_from_sim$stats_all
```

When using simulations for method checking, compare the fitted model with the
known data-generating model. When using simulations for teaching, show both the
underlying curve (`y`) and the noisy observations (`random_y`) so users can
distinguish the epidemic process from the observation process.
